rv.q: The revival of Michael Frayn's 'Noises Off' that opened Sunday at the Roundabout Theatre Company's Theatre is every bit as funny as you've heard—and then some.

The production particulars, like Derek McClane’s set and Michael Krass’s suitably silly costumes, are spot on, but the actors don’t quite seem to be in the same play or even the same play within a play.

Or you could blame the material itself: Is Noises Off—with its deconstructed Benny Hill Show sight gags and bravura layering of in-the-wings "reality" onto fictional stage business—too tired and possibly overrated?
If you're looking for a night of gut-busting hilarity, you can't do any better than this one.
And this production at Roundabout’s Theatre ensures that we do, in just the right spirit.

"A percussive dose of slamming doors, wince-inducing pratfalls and enough suggestive tomfoolery to fill the bill at Minsky’s…Jeremy Herrin lets 'Noises Off' wind up a bit slowly, but once all the gears are in synch, the show is a dazzlement of set-pieces fit together with jigsaw perfection.
The direction, performances, and set design by Derek McLane create a symphony of shouting and flop sweat, turning pure slapstick into high art.
But a great production, which this revival certainly is, builds the slapstick around truthful performances, thus making the chaos feel natural.

"There are several surprising things about Roundabout’s revival of Michael Frayn’s 1982 madcap farce. The first is almost consistent laughter erupting somewhere in the audience over the course of three acts (with one intermission). Three acts without a slump in energy or imagination.
I think you’ll find it on 42nd Street by visiting Michael Frayn’s irreverently funny farce.

In this live answer to a biopic, young Gloria’s life changes when she impresses music wiz Emilio Estefan, though as their joint career burgeons, she gets resistance from mama, who (shades of Gypsy) is still hurting from dashed show biz dreams of her own.
For the most part this cast has these characters buttoned down tighter than a ship’s canvas.
All you have to do as the audience is sit back and enjoy an hysterical evening of high jinks in the theatre.
Roundabout Theatre Company's revival has a lot going for it.
There were plenty of stars in this production although none of them shone overly brightly.

It must be almost heartwarming to share in the hilarity in a closed space; such a reaction en masse is just a slightly alienating experience for those of us who can’t help viewing this three-decade-old farce as little more than The Three Stooges with a British accent.
Consequently, though the production is entertaining for its comic portrayals, it fails to trigger all the laughs inherent in the script or become the laugh riot it is intended to be.
Therefore my negative response to this production is based largely on seeing an ensemble of expert farceurs led astray by a director who apparently didn’t believe that less is more.
